title: Not without God: the lives Jesus changed
source_text: Ἴδωμεν δὲ τίνα τρόπον συκοφαντεῖ Ἰουδαίους ὁ πάντ᾿ ἐπαγγελλόμενος εἰδέναι Κέλσος, λέγων αὐτοὺς σέβειν ἀγγέλους καὶ γοητείᾳ προσκεῖσθαι. ἧς ὁ Μω(??)σῆς αὐτοῖς γέγονεν ἐξηγητής. ποῦ γὰρ τῶν γραμμάτων Μω(??)σέως εὗρε τὸν νομοθέτην παραδιδόντα σέβειν ἀγγέλους. λεγέτω ὁ ἐπαγγελλόμενος εἰδέναι τὰ Χριστιανῶν καὶ Ἰουδαίων, πῶς δὲ καὶ γοητεία παρὰ τοῖς παραδεξαμένοις τὸν Μωϋσέως νόμον ἐστὶν. ἀνεγνωκόσι καὶ τὸ „τοῖς ἐπαοιδοῖς οὐ προσκολληθήσεσθε ἐκμιανθῆναι ἐν αὐτοῖς“; ἐπαγγέλλεται δὲ διδάξειν ἑξῆς, πῶς καὶ Ἰουσαῖοι ὑπὸ ἀμαθίας ἐσφάλησαν ἐξαπατώμενοι. καὶ εἰ μὲν ηὕρισκε τὴν περὶ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐν Ἰουδαίοις ἀμαθίαν. μὴ κατακούσ ασιτῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ προφητειῶν. ἀληθῶς ἂν ἐδίδαξε. πῶς ἐσφάλησαν Ἰουδαῖοι· νῦν δὲ ταῦτα οὐδὲ βουληθεὶς φαντασθῆναι τὰ μὴ σφάλματα Ἰουδαίων σφάλματα εἶναι ὑπολαμβάνει. ἐπαγγειλάμενος δ᾿ ὁ Κέλσος ὕστερον διδάξειν τὰ περὶ Ἰουδαίων. πρῶτον ποιεῖται τὸν λόγον περὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν. ὡς γενομένου ἡγεμόνος τῇ καθὸ Χριστιανοί ἐσμεν γενέσει ἡμῶν. καί φησιν αὐτὸν πρὸ πάνυ ὀλίγων ἐτῶν τῆς διδασκαλίας ταύτης καθηγήσασθαι. νομισθέντα ὑπὸ Χριστιανῶν υἱὸν εἶναι τοῦ θεοῦ. καὶ περὶ αὐτοῦ δὲ τοῦ πρὸ ὀλίγων ἐτῶν αὐτὸν γεγονέναι τοιαῦτα φήσομεν· ἆρα τὸ ἐν τοσούτοις ἔτεσι βουληθέντα σπεῖραι τὸν ἑαυτοῦ λόγον καὶ διδασκαλίαν τὸν Ἰησοῦν τοσοῦτον δεδυνῆσθαι, ὡς πολλαχοῦ τῆς καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς οἰκουμένης διατεθῆναι πρὸς τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ οὐκ ὀλίγους Ἕλληνας καὶ βαρβάρους, σοφοὺς καὶ ἀνοήτους, ὥστε μέχρι θανάτου ἀγωνίζεσθαι ὑπὲρ χριστιανισμοῦ, ἵν᾿ αὐτὸν μὴ ἐξομόσωνται, ὅπερ οὐδεὶς ὑπὲρ ἄλλου δόγματος ἱστόρηται ποιεῖν, ἀθεεὶ γεγένηται; ἐγὼ μὲν οὖν οὐ κολακεύων τὸν λόγον ἀλλὰ πειρώμενος τεθεωρημένως ἐξετάζειν τὰ πράγματα φήσαιμι ἂν ὅτι οὐδ᾿ οἱ σώματα πολλὰ κάμνοντα θεραπεύοντες ἀθεεὶ τυγχάνουσι τοῦ κατὰ τὴν ὑγίειαν τῶν σωμάτων τέλους· εἰ δὲ καὶ ψυχάς τις δύναιτο ἀπαλλάττειν τῆς κατὰ τὴν κακίαν χύσεως καὶ ἀκολαστημάτων καὶ ἀδικοπραγημάτων καὶ τῆς περὶ τὸ θεῖον καταφρονήσεως, καὶ δεῖξιν διδοίη τοῦ τοιούτου ἔργου βελτιωθέντας τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἑκατὸν (ἔστω γὰρ ἐπὶ τοσούτων ὁ λόγος), οὐδὲ τοῦτον ἂν εὐλόγως φήσαι τις οὐκ ἀθεεὶ λόγον τοσούτων κακῶν ἀπαλλακτικὸν ἐμπεποιηκέναι τοῖς ἑκατόν; εἰ δ᾿ ὁ εὐγνωμόνως ταῦτα κατανοῶν συγκαταθήσεται τῷ μηδὲν κρεῖττον ἐν ἀνθρώποις γεγονέναι ἀθεεὶ. πόσῳ πλέον τὸ τοσοῦτον περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ θαῤῥῶν ἀποφανεῖται, συνεξετάζων πολλῶν προσερχομένων αὐτοῦ τῷ λόγῳ ἀρχαιοτέρους βίους μεταγενεστέροις καὶ κατανοῶν, ἐν ὅσαις μὲν ἀκολασίαις ὅσαις δὲ ἀδικίαις καὶ πλεονεξίαις ἕκαστος τῶνδε ἦν. πρὶν, ὥς φησι Κέλσος καὶ οἱ τὰ αὐτὰ αὐτῷ νομίζοντες, ἀπατηθῶσι καὶ παραδέξωνται λόγον λυμαινόμενον, ὡς ἐκεῖνοι λέγουσι. τὸν τῶν ἀνθρώπων βίον, ἐξ οὗ δὲ παρειλήφασι τὸν λόγον, τίνα τρόπον γεγόνασιν ἐπιεικέστεροι καὶ σεμνότεροι καὶ εὐσταθέστεροι, ὥς τινας αὐτῶν διὰ τὸν ἔρωτα τῆς ὑπερβαλλούσης καθαρότητος καὶ διὰ τὸ καθαρώτερον θρησκεύειν τὸ θεῖον μηδὲ τῶν συγκεχωρημένων ὑπὸ τοῦ νόμου ἅπτεσθαι ἀφροδισίων;
pass_a_gloss: Let us see in what way Celsus, the one professing (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) to know (οἶδα) all things, slanders (συκοφαντέω) Jews, saying they worship (σέβω) angels (ἄγγελοι) and are devoted (πρόσκειμαι) to sorcery (γοητεία), of which Moses became their expounder (ἐξηγητής). For where in the writings (γράμματα) of Moses did he find the lawgiver (νομοθέτης) handing down (παραδίδωμι) to worship angels? Let him say, the one professing to know the things of Christians and Jews; and how is sorcery among those who accepted (παραδέχομαι) the law (νόμος) of Moses, having also read (ἀναγιγνώσκω) 'to the enchanters (ἐπαοιδοί) you shall not be joined (προσκολλάομαι, fut. pass.) to be defiled (ἐκμιαίνω) by them'? He professes he will teach (διδάσκω) next how also Jews went astray (σφάλλω, aor. pass.) through ignorance (ἀμαθία), being deceived (ἐξαπατάω). And if he were finding (εὑρίσκω, impf., unreal) the ignorance among Jews about Jesus the Christ, not having heeded (κατακούω, neg.) the prophecies (προφητεῖαι) about him, truly he would have taught how Jews went astray; but now, not even having wished to imagine (φαντάζομαι) these things, he supposes (ὑπολαμβάνω) the non-errors (σφάλματα) of Jews to be errors. Having professed that later he will teach the things about Jews, Celsus first makes his account (λόγος) about our Saviour (σωτήρ), as having become leader (ἡγεμών) of our coming-to-be (γένεσις) insofar as (καθό) we are Christians; and says he very few years before led (καθηγέομαι) this teaching (διδασκαλία), thought (νομίζω, aor. pass. ptc.) by Christians to be Son of God. And about this very thing, his having come into being (γίνομαι) a few years ago, we shall say such things: is it godlessly / without God (ἀθεεί) that Jesus, having wished in so [few] years (ἐν τοσούτοις ἔτεσι) to sow (σπείρω) his word (λόγος) and teaching, has been so able (δύναμαι, pf.) that in many places of the inhabited world (οἰκουμένη) according to us not few Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish (ἀνόητοι), have been disposed (διατίθημι, aor. pass.) toward his word, so as to contend (ἀγωνίζομαι) unto death on behalf of Christianity in order not to forswear (ἐξόμνυμι) him, which no one is recorded (ἱστορέω) to do on behalf of another doctrine (δόγμα)? I then, not flattering (κολακεύω) the word but attempting to examine (ἐξετάζω) the facts reflectively (τεθεωρημένως), would say that not even those healing (θεραπεύω) many suffering (κάμνω) bodies attain (τυγχάνω) without God the end (τέλος) of bodily health (ὑγίεια); and if one could release (ἀπαλλάττω) souls from the outpouring/dissolution (χύσις) according to vice (κακία), and from licentious acts (ἀκολαστήματα) and unjust deeds (ἀδικοπραγήματα) and contempt (καταφρόνησις) of the divine (τὸ θεῖον), and give a proof (δεῖξις) of such work, those improved (βελτιόω) in number a hundred (let the argument be about so many), would not one reasonably (εὐλόγως) say also this one not without God implanted (ἐμποιέω, pf.) in the hundred a word able to release (ἀπαλλακτικός) from so many evils? And if the one considering these things fairly (εὐγνωμόνως) will agree (συγκατατίθεμαι) that nothing better has come to be among men without God, how much more will he boldly (θαρρῶν) declare (ἀποφαίνομαι) so much (τὸ τοσοῦτον) about Jesus, examining together (συνεξετάζω) the earlier lives (βίοι) of many coming to his word with the later, and considering in how many licentiousnesses (ἀκολασίαι), how many injustices (ἀδικίαι) and greeds (πλεονεξίαι) each of these was, before, as Celsus says and those thinking the same as he, they were deceived (ἀπατάω) and accepted a word corrupting (λυμαίνομαι), as those say, the life of men; and from the time they received the word, in what way they have become more gentle (ἐπιεικέστεροι) and more dignified (σεμνότεροι) and more stable (εὐσταθέστεροι), so that some of them, through love (ἔρως) of surpassing (ὑπερβάλλω) purity (καθαρότης) and through worshipping (θρησκεύω) the divine more purely, do not even touch (ἅπτομαι) the sexual pleasures (ἀφροδίσια) permitted (συγχωρέω) by the law.
pass_b_english: Let us see how Celsus, who professes to know everything, slanders the Jews when he says that they "worship angels and are given to sorcery, in which Moses was their instructor." Where in the writings of Moses did he find the lawgiver handing down the worship of angels? Let him say, since he professes to know the teachings of Christians and Jews. And how is there sorcery among those who have accepted the law of Moses, and who have also read, "You shall not attach yourselves to enchanters, to be defiled by them" (Leviticus 19:31)? He promises to teach next how the Jews too went astray through ignorance and were deceived. Had he found ignorance among the Jews about Jesus the Christ, in that they did not heed the prophecies about him, he would truly have taught how the Jews went astray. As it is, without even caring to imagine these things, he takes for errors of the Jews what are not errors.

Celsus promises to teach about the Jews later, but first he makes his argument about our Saviour, as the one who led the way in our coming to be Christians. He says that "he became the leader of this teaching a very few years ago, and was thought by Christians to be the Son of God." On this very point, that he came a few years ago, we shall say this. Is it without God that Jesus, wishing in so few years to sow his word and teaching, has been able to do so much that in many parts of our inhabited world not a few Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish, have become so devoted to his word that they struggle even to death for Christianity rather than forswear him, which no one is recorded to have done for any other doctrine?

For my part, not flattering our teaching but trying to examine the facts with careful thought, I would say that not even those who heal many sick bodies reach the goal of bodily health without God. And if someone could free souls from the dissipation of vice, from licentious and unjust deeds, and from contempt for the divine, and could give as proof of such work a hundred people made better (let the argument be about that many), would not anyone reasonably say of him too that it was not without God that he had implanted in those hundred a word able to free them from so many evils? And if one who weighs these things fairly will grant that nothing better has come about among men without God, how much more confidently will he declare as much of Jesus, when he compares the former lives of many who come to his word with their later lives, and considers in how much licentiousness, how much injustice and greed each of them lived before they were "deceived", as Celsus and those who share his views say, and accepted a teaching which, as those men say, ruins human life; and how, from the time they received the word, they have become gentler, more dignified and steadier, so that some of them, for love of surpassing purity and for the sake of worshipping the divine more purely, do not even touch the sexual relations that the law permits.

choices.choice: Leviticus 19:31 is quoted from the Septuagint (καὶ τοῖς ἐπαοιδοῖς οὐ προσκολληθήσεσθε ἐκμιανθῆναι ἐν αὐτοῖς), matching the English verse number. Read Ἰουδαῖοι for the TEI's Ἰουσαῖοι, and μὴ κατακούσασι τῶν for the garbled μὴ κατακούσ ασιτῶν. Celsus's charge ('worship angels ... instructor') and his claim about Jesus ('became the leader ... Son of God') are in indirect speech but keep his wording, so they are put in quotation marks; 'deceived' (ἀπατηθῶσι) is marked as Celsus's word. ἡγεμόνος τῇ καθὸ Χριστιανοί ἐσμεν γενέσει ἡμῶν rendered 'the one who led the way in our coming to be, insofar as we are Christians'. ἐν τοσούτοις ἔτεσι taken as 'in so few years', picking up Celsus's 'a very few years'. ἀθεεί = 'without God'. χύσις (literally 'pouring out, dissolution') rendered 'dissipation'. The double negative οὐδὲ ... οὐκ ἀθεεί in the rhetorical question is resolved as 'would not anyone say it was not without God'. 'The sexual relations that the law permits' (τῶν συγκεχωρημένων ὑπὸ τοῦ νόμου ἀφροδισίων) refers to lawful marriage; possible background in 1 Corinthians 7:1–9, 32–35, left uncited. The TEI full stops after ἐξηγητής, ἀγγέλους, ἐστίν, ἀμαθίαν, προφητειῶν, ἐδίδαξε, Ἰουδαίων, ἡμῶν, ταύτης, θεοῦ, ἀθεεί, ἦν and λέγουσι are construed across.
stiff order 'supposes to be errors of the Jews what are not errors' -> 'takes for errors of the Jews what are not errors'; 'did not even wish to picture' -> 'without even caring to imagine'
'led the way in our coming to be, insofar as we are Christians' -> 'in our coming to be Christians'
removed addition 'only' twice (πρὸ πάνυ ὀλίγων / πρὸ ὀλίγων ἐτῶν)
restored οὐδὲ τοῦτον: 'say of him too that it was not without God'
placed Celsus's 'deceived' beside its own clause (πρὶν ... ἀπατηθῶσι)
διὰ τὸ καθαρώτερον θρησκεύειν: 'in order to' -> 'for the sake of'
checked Leviticus 19:31 against the Septuagint wording quoted
